policeViolence: Told by a guy who has been on both sides of the shield — and has the bruises and the coffee stains to prove it Don't Hit Grandma With A Sign: How We Stop Police Violence Against Peaceful Manifestations A story in 12 chapters. Funny where it hurts, serious where it counts. If you are a protester, a cop, a mayor, or just someone who pays taxes for helmets to be banged against placards — this is for you. 1. The Square Where Nothing Dangerous Happened (Until The Vans Arrived) Let me tell you how it started, because I was there, with bad shoes and a borrowed sign. Tuesday, 6pm, Republic Square. Or Liberty Square. Honestly every city has the same square — pigeons, a closed kiosk, a statue of a guy on a horse who nobody can name. There were maybe 300 of us. Nurses asking for overtime pay. A couple teachers. Students with too much eyeliner and too little sleep. Dona Lurdes with her cookies. A kid with a drum who could not keep rhythm to save his life. Signs like “WE CAN’T BREATHE ON THESE WAGES” and “MY GRANDMA MARCHES FASTER THAN REFORM.” Dangerous stuff. Extremely dangerous cardboard. We chanted. Badly. Someone started “The people united” and half forgot the words and mumbled. A dog slept through it. A street vendor sold water at double price — capitalism survived the protest just fine. Then you heard them. Not chanting. Engines. Three vans, doors sliding like in movies. Shields, helmets, boots that cost more than my month’s rent. They lined up like we were an invading army. I swear the pigeons were more threatening that day — one actually stole a cop’s sandwich later, true story. Nothing had been broken. Nothing thrown. The only thing in the air was sweat and cheap sunscreen. But the line advanced. And that’s the first lesson I want tattooed on every city hall wall: peace does not break by itself. Someone has to come break it. I’m not an AI writing from a cloud. I’m a man who carried his neighbor’s kid on his shoulders that day because the kid wanted to see. I remember the smell of popcorn from the corner. I remember thinking: if anyone hits anyone here, it won’t be us starting it. We didn’t even have sticks for the signs — they were taped to cardboard tubes so we wouldn’t poke anyone’s eye out. That’s how hardcore we were. 2. Meet Officer Robocop Brain-Optional and His Magic Baton Okay, I’m going to make fun now. Forgive me, but some of it you earn. Every deployment has a Robocop Brain-Optional. You know him. Visor down even though it’s 34 degrees. Chest out. Baton twirling like he’s in a Michael Bay film. He didn’t join to protect. He joined because he liked the uniform in the mirror and because his cousin said you get respect without having to earn it. Field guide to Brain-Optional (subspecies: Escudus erectus ): Identified by shouting “MOVE BACK!” at people who are sitting. Believes a grandma with a Tupperware is a logistical threat. Thinks cameras are weapons. Thinks thinking is disobedience. His baton is magic: one tap turns a nurse into a “rioter,” a student into a “threat,” and his own paycheck into a lawsuit the city will pay, not him. That Tuesday, Brain-Optional found his nemesis: Dona Lurdes. She offered him a cookie. I saw it. “Son, you look hot, eat.” He shouted “DO NOT APPROACH!” She’s 68, 1.58m, approach speed: glacier. He pushed her sign. The sign said “COOKIES FOR FAIR WAGES.” Extremely subversive pastry. Here’s the provocative part, and I mean it: if your threat assessment flags cookies, you are not in security. You are in comedy. And it’s expensive comedy. One shove, one old lady on the ground, ten phones filming, and boom — you just turned 300 peaceful nobodies into 30,000 angry somebodies by tomorrow. Congratulations, genius. You created the danger you were sent to prevent. I’m not saying all cops are like this. I’m saying the ones who are, are loud, hit first, and hide behind the good ones when the video goes viral. And commanders love them until the lawsuit, then they’ve “never seen this officer before in their lives.” 3. Anatomy of Stupidity: Why Beating Peaceful People Is Tactically Idiotic Let me put my teacher hat on, because this story has to teach something useful or it’s just bar talk. Beating a peaceful manifestation is stupid on five levels. Write them down: 1. It doesn’t work. You don’t disperse ideas with bruises. You water them. Every textbook on crowd psychology — and every grandma — knows this. Hit a sitting kid and his entire school shows up next day. Gas a square and you get three squares. 2. It’s expensive. Overtime, medical bills, broken shields, lawsuits, burnt vans next week when people actually get mad. The city pays. That means you pay, even if you cheered for the beating on TV. The baton always bills the taxpayer. 3. It blinds you. Once you start hitting, you can’t tell who is actually dangerous. The one guy who did bring a Molotov hides behind the chaos you created. Good policing is like good surgery: don’t cut everything because one tooth is rotten. 4. It corrupts rookies. The 22-year-old who joined to help finds himself ordered to shove a teacher. He either obeys and hates himself, or disobeys and gets punished. You just taught him law is about obedience, not justice. Ten years later he’s Brain-Optional 2.0. 5. It’s cowardly math. 20 armored cops vs. one kid with a drum is not bravery. Real bravery is standing between traffic and marchers so nobody gets run over. Real bravery is telling your lieutenant “sir, these people are sitting, there’s no lawful reason to charge.” Kid with drum to cop line: “Why are you in armor? We’re not even in tune.” Cop (honest one, whispering): “Tell me about it. I told them we needed water, not shields.” Peaceful crowds are not dangerous. They are inconvenient. They block traffic. They chant off-key. They make politicians uncomfortable. Inconvenience is not danger. If your training confuses the two, your training is the danger. 4. Meet Dona Lurdes, 68, Terrorist Threat Level: Cookies Dona Lurdes is real. I changed her name a little because she’d kill me if I put her address, but everything else is true. Retired cook, widow, knees bad, voice loud. She brings cookies to every march because “people with low sugar make bad decisions — including police.” When Brain-Optional pushed her, she did not throw a brick. She sat down harder. Gravity as resistance. Then she said the most dangerous sentence of the day: “Son, I pay your salary, and I’m disappointed.” Ten phones caught it. That line did more damage to violent policing than any barricade. Humor is a weapon here, and I mean it as tactic: peaceful ridicule exposes stupidity without giving excuse for beating. When cops in armor face grandmas with cookies, who looks strong? Not the armor. My advice to every march: bring grandmas to the front. Not as shields — as mirrors. No officer wants to explain to his own mother why he pepper-sprayed someone’s mother over cardboard. Dona Lurdes later filed a complaint. With receipt for cookies. “Item: 40 cookies, wasted due to shove.” The clerk laughed, then stamped it. Paper is slow, but paper remembers when bruises fade. Keep receipts. Literally. 5. The Other Cop: Mario, Who Reads Orders Twice Now the other side, because I promised, and because it’s true. Mario is 41, two kids, belly from station coffee, 17 years on the force. He was in that line too. Helmet under arm because “if I can’t see faces, I can’t do my job.” When lieutenant shouted “Push them back to the avenue,” Mario did something revolutionary: he looked. He saw kids sitting. Signs. Cookies on pavement. No bricks, no bottles, no knives. He leaned to the rookie next to him: “What exactly are we pushing? Air?” Then he did the four-word magic: walked to lieutenant and said, “Is that lawful, sir?” I didn’t hear it — a journalist friend told me later, and Mario confirmed over beer (he paid, good man). The lieutenant blinked. “It’s an order.” Mario: “Orders need legal basis, sir. What’s the infraction? Assembly is constitutional. No violence, no blockade of emergency route — we can reroute traffic in ten minutes. If we charge, we create the crime.” That pause saved the day from becoming a hospital night. The lieutenant, to his credit, hesitated. Hesitation is underrated. He radioed: “Hold line. No advance unless attacked.” Brain-Optional sulked. Mario handed Dona Lurdes back her Tupperware. Listen: police are useful — essential, even — but only when they question orders. A cop who obeys blindly is just a baton with legs. A cop who thinks is a citizen with authority. The first serves whoever shouts loudest. The second serves law. Lesson from Mario for every cop reading this (and I know some are): Your oath is to the constitution, not to the lieutenant’s mood. “I was following orders” stopped working as an excuse in 1945. If an order tells you to beat peaceful people, that order is unlawful. Refusing it is not disobedience — it’s obedience to higher law. And yes, it takes guts. So does getting hit with a brick, and you signed up for guts. 6. Useful Police 101: What Cops Are Actually For (Hint: Not Piñata Duty) Let’s be provocative but fair: we need police. I need them. You need them. The street vendor needs them when someone actually robs him. The march needs them when a drunk driver tries to plow through. My daughter needs them when she walks home at night. But useful police at a peaceful manifestation do four boring, beautiful things: 1. Protect the march from traffic and from provocateurs. Stand on the edges, backs to protesters, eyes outward. The best cop at a demo is the one you barely notice because he’s stopping cars, not swinging. 2. Talk. “Hey, organizers, where are you heading? Let’s keep one lane open for ambulances, deal?” Ten minutes of talk saves ten hours of ER. Mario does this. Brain-Optional thinks talking is weakness. Talking is tactics. 3. Target only real violence, precisely. If one idiot throws a bottle, you pull that idiot — with minimum force, on camera — not gas the 299 others. Collective punishment is for bad parents, not professionals. 4. Document for truth. Bodycams on. Not off when it gets interesting. A good cop wants footage because footage proves he was good. I once saw Mario carry that kid-with-drum’s drum over a puddle so it wouldn’t get wet. The crowd laughed, clapped. Next chant was “MARIO! MARIO!” He blushed under his cap. That’s authority. Not fear — trust. Fear needs armor. Trust just needs consistency. So yeah, mock the stupid, but recruit the useful. When you chant “cops are...” — finish it with “welcome if they protect.” It confuses Brain-Optional and delights Mario. Provocation with precision. 7. The Order: “Disperse Them” — And The Four Words That Save Lives Every abuse starts with vague words on a radio. “Disperse.” “Clear.” “Restore order.” Order of what? There was order — sitting order, singing order. Here’s what I teach in workshops now (yes, I do them in community halls with bad coffee, come): For cops: the 30-second legality check. 1. What law is being broken, specifically? (Noise after 10pm is not “riot.” Sitting is not “attack.”) 2. Is my action proportionate and necessary? (Baton vs. cardboard = no. Shield wall vs. sitting = no.) 3. Did I warn clearly, give time and exit path? (“Disperse in 2 minutes via north street, water station there” — not a scream while charging.) 4. Would I do this if my mother and my chief were both filming? (They are. Phones everywhere.) If any answer is no — hold, ask, document refusal of unlawful order. Write it. Paper protects thinkers. Mario told me his trick: he repeats the order back loudly. “Sir, confirm: you want us to use force against seated, non-violent people with no emergency blockade?” Nine times out of ten, the commander rephrases to something lawful, because now it’s on record. Bureaucracy, used for good. Beautiful. And commanders: if you give an order you wouldn’t sign with your name in the newspaper tomorrow, don’t give it. “Just clear them, I don’t care how” means “I want violence without responsibility.” Courts translate that now. So do mothers. 8. What Protesters Can Do So Even Dumb Policing Fails Story time again, because preaching bores even me. After the cookie incident, we got smart. Not paranoid — organized. Old Man Joaquim, ex-army, became our “Mario on our side.” He taught: Know the line. March permit? Route? Time? Print it. Give copy to police liaison. When you’re clearly legal, unlawful orders stand out like a baton in a bakery. De-escalation team with vests. Our team wore yellow vests: “PEACE TEAM.” Their job: hug the hotheads (metaphorically), talk down the drunk guy, pull back the kid who wants to throw. They also filmed everything — two phones per team, power banks, livestream. Brain-Optional hates livestream the way vampires hate garlic. Grandmas front, sound truck middle, medics back. Front line sitting if charged. Hands up, palms open. Chant: “We are peaceful — film this.” It’s hard to beat people chanting they’re peaceful while sitting. It looks exactly like what it is. No masks for throwing, no sticks, no bottles. We banned them ourselves. Anyone masked and throwing was isolated — our peace team pointed: “That guy is not with us.” That denies police the excuse of “mixed violent crowd.” It also protects us from infiltrators who love a good smash. Talk to Mario before march. We started meeting the station a day before. “We’ll be 500, route X, end 8pm, our liaison is Ana with red cap, yours?” Most cops relaxed visibly. Only Brain-Optional was disappointed — no war, no story for the bar. Ana (red cap) to line: “Officers, we’ll keep right lane free, kids in middle, we end at 8, okay?” Mario: “Deal. I’ll put two guys at the intersection so buses pass.” Brain-Optional: “...” (kicking pebble, dreaming of riot) Useful lesson: discipline is our shield. Humor is our sword. Cameras are our witnesses. Paper is our revenge. 9. What Commanders Fear More Than Bricks: Cameras, Grandmas, and Paperwork Let me be blunt, human to human: commanders don’t fear your chant. They fear your folder. After Dona Lurdes fell, Ana did three things that night that scared the station more than any brick: uploaded video with time-stamp, took Lurdes to clinic for a report (bruise, shock), and filed a complaint with number, names, badge numbers she’d memorized by flirting with Mario (“for the report, handsome, your badge?” — he laughed and gave it, because good cops aren’t afraid of names). That folder grew: 12 videos, 3 medical reports, 1 cookie receipt, 40 witness contacts. It went to the ombudsman, the press, the councilwoman. The lieutenant who ordered “push” got called to explain. Brain-Optional got “reassigned to traffic” — which is where he now tickets pigeons, allegedly. Provocative truth: one grandma with a folder beats ten kids with stones. Stones give excuse. Folders give consequences. Be the folder. And cops, listen: the folder protects you too. Mario’s bodycam and written “Is that lawful, sir?” saved him when the inquiry came. The inquiry saw who held line and who pushed. Paper distinguishes Mario from Brain-Optional when headlines blur. If you’re good, you want more paper, not less. 10. The Night Nobody Got Hit — A Manual in Story Form Three months later, same square, 2000 people now — because stupidity recruits. Big march. Everyone expected war. Vans again. Same lieutenant, wiser. Same Mario, calmer. Same Brain-Optional, traffic cone in hand. What happened? Boring. Gloriously boring. 5pm: Ana meets lieutenant, hands route, liaison numbers. Lieutenant: “North street must stay open for hospital.” Ana: “Done, our yellow vests will keep it.” Mario nods. 6pm: March starts. Peace team in yellow. Grandmas front with cookies (extra for cops — diplomacy via sugar). Medics back with red crosses. Livestreamers on ladders. 6:40pm: One masked kid throws a bottle. Misses. Our peace team surrounds him, takes bottle, points to police: “Him, not us. We’ll testify.” Mario’s squad pulls him precisely, no gas, no charge. Crowd claps. Yes, claps for an arrest — because it was fair. 7:30pm: Provocateur shouts “Pigs!” in Mario’s face, spitting. Mario: “Sir, step back, you’re free to shout from there.” No baton. Spit wiped. Dignity kept. The crowd chants “MA-RI-O!” The provocateur looks stupid, leaves. 8pm: Ends on time. Trash picked up by us (revolutionary hygiene). Lieutenant on radio: “Crowd dispersing voluntarily. No force used.” He sounds almost disappointed and relieved at once. No one hit. No one gassed. Traffic resumed. Cookies shared. Pigeons fed. Manual hidden in story: Liaison + legal route + internal discipline + precise policing + cameras + humor = boring night. Boring is victory. If you want exciting protests, let Brain-Optional command. If you want change, be boring and relentless. Power hates boring persistence more than exciting riots — riots end, persistence votes, sues, elects. I cried a little that night, not ashamed to say. Not from gas. From relief. My neighbor’s kid on shoulders again, waving at Mario. Mario waving back. That’s the country I want. 11. Law Without Latin: Your Rights, Their Limits, and The Paper That Bites Back I’m not a lawyer — I’m a guy who got tired of being shoved and read stuff at 2am. So plain words, check your local law because I’m not your lawyer: Peaceful assembly is a right, not a favor. Constitutions and human rights treaties protect it. Police need a real, specific, lawful reason to limit it — imminent violence, blocking ER access with no alternative — not “inconvenience” or “we don’t like chant.” Force must be legal, necessary, proportionate, warned. Baton against sitting = disproportionate. Gas without exit = trap. Shooting rubber at faces = crime. Orders to do those = unlawful — must be questioned, refused, reported. Film. In public you can generally film police doing duty. Keep distance, don’t interfere, state “I’m filming, not interfering.” Livestream so deletion fails. Badge numbers, times, streets — narrate them aloud on video. Complain fast, complain precise. Date, hour, place, badge, what happened, witnesses, medical report within 24h, keep clothes, keep cookie receipts. Ombudsman, prosecutor, press, council — same folder to all.
